title: Spring Boot
description: Build and test a production-style REST API with Spring Boot, and understand the "magic" (dependency injection, auto-configuration) well enough to debug it. Java 17+, Spring Boot 3 and 4.
keyIdeas: Spring Boot = Spring + **starters** + **auto-configuration** + an **embedded server**: `@SpringBootApplication` scans your package, configures what your classpath needs, and `java -jar` runs it.
Your classes become **beans** through annotations like `@Service`; ask for dependencies through one constructor, and remember every bean is a shared singleton.
Auto-configuration is conditional `@Bean` definitions: tune it with properties, override it by defining your own bean, and debug it with `debug=true`.

A REST endpoint is a `@RestController` method: input via `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam` and `@Valid @RequestBody`, output as records or a `ResponseEntity`, errors mapped once in a `@RestControllerAdvice` returning `ProblemDetail`.
Spring Data JPA turns `interface CustomerRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long>` and names like `findByEmail` into working queries.
One jar for every environment: profiles and environment variables change the config, and test slices (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`) keep tests fast.

concepts.label: Starter
concepts.summary: One starter dependency pulls in a tested set of libraries, and Boot's dependency management pins their versions for you.

concepts.label: Embedded server
concepts.summary: The web server (Tomcat by default, port 8080) ships inside an executable jar, so java -jar is all production needs.

concepts.label: Component scanning
concepts.summary: @SpringBootApplication scans its own package and sub-packages for annotated classes and registers them as beans; sibling packages are missed.

concepts.label: Dependency injection
concepts.summary: A class declares what it needs and the application context (IoC container) supplies it, instead of the class building its own dependencies.

concepts.label: Bean
concepts.summary: An object created and managed by the Spring container, one shared instance by default, declared with @Component/@Service/... or a @Bean method.

concepts.label: Constructor injection
concepts.summary: Receiving dependencies through the constructor makes them final and visible and lets tests just call new, unlike field @Autowired.

concepts.label: Auto-configuration
concepts.summary: Boot registers beans from conditional configuration classes based on what is on the classpath and backs off (@ConditionalOnMissingBean) when you define your own.

concepts.label: Properties
concepts.summary: Keys in application.properties or .yml tune auto-configuration (server.port, spring.*) and bind your own settings via @ConfigurationProperties; unknown keys are silently ignored.

concepts.label: Ambiguous beans
concepts.summary: Spring injects by type, so two matching beans fail startup until @Primary, @Qualifier or a List of all of them resolves the choice.

concepts.label: Circular dependency
concepts.summary: Beans that need each other through their constructors can never be built, so startup fails; split out the shared logic.

concepts.label: @RestController
concepts.summary: A controller whose handler methods map HTTP routes and return objects that Jackson writes as the JSON response body.

concepts.label: Request binding
concepts.summary: @PathVariable, @RequestParam and @RequestBody turn path segments, query parameters and JSON bodies into method arguments (usually records, i.e. DTOs).

concepts.label: HTTP status codes
concepts.summary: A returned object means 200, ResponseEntity sets others such as 201 or 404, and Spring answers 400 for bad input and 500 for unhandled exceptions.

concepts.label: Bean Validation
concepts.summary: Constraint annotations like @NotBlank and @Min on a DTO are checked only when the parameter (and any nested object) is marked @Valid; failures give 400.

concepts.label: Exception handler
concepts.summary: @ExceptionHandler methods in a @RestControllerAdvice turn exceptions into responses such as a ProblemDetail; the most specific handler wins.

concepts.label: JPA entity
concepts.summary: An @Entity class with an @Id maps to a table, and Hibernate only creates or changes the schema if ddl-auto says so.

concepts.label: Spring Data repository
concepts.summary: An interface extending JpaRepository gets save/findById plus queries derived from method names, or written with @Query, generated at startup.

concepts.label: Profiles
concepts.summary: A profile such as dev or prod is a named file of overrides (application-{profile}.properties) that applies only when that profile is active.

concepts.label: Property precedence
concepts.summary: Command-line arguments beat environment variables, which beat profile files, which beat application.properties; env vars use relaxed binding (SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL).

concepts.label: @Transactional
concepts.summary: A proxy around the bean opens a transaction and rolls back on unchecked exceptions only; internal this-calls skip the proxy.

concepts.label: N+1 problem
concepts.summary: Loading a list and then touching a lazy association on each item fires one query plus one per row; a fetch join or entity graph loads it in one.

concepts.label: Slice test
concepts.summary: @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest starts only one layer, so collaborators outside it are replaced with @MockitoBean mocks.

concepts.label: Security filter chain
concepts.summary: Adding Spring Security locks every endpoint; a SecurityFilterChain bean lists request rules that are checked in order, first match wins.

concepts.label: Actuator
concepts.summary: Production endpoints under /actuator, where health answers 200 UP or 503 DOWN and only health is exposed over HTTP by default.

units.title: How Spring Boot works
units.description: What Spring Boot adds on top of Spring, how dependency injection wires your app, and what auto-configuration is really doing.

lessons.title: Spring vs Spring Boot: what you actually get
lessons.takeaway: Spring is the framework; Spring Boot adds starters, auto-configuration and an embedded server, so running `main()` (or `java -jar`) starts a complete web app.

steps.title: Spring, then Spring Boot
steps.body:
**Spring Framework** is a toolkit for Java back ends: a dependency-injection container plus modules for web (Spring MVC), data access, transactions, security and more. Before Boot, you configured much of it by hand and deployed a WAR file to a separately installed server.

**Spring Boot** sits on top of Spring and makes the boring choices for you:

- **Starters**: one dependency such as `spring-boot-starter-web` pulls in a tested set of libraries (Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON, embedded Tomcat).
- **Auto-configuration**: it looks at your classpath and properties and creates sensible beans for you.
- **Embedded server**: the web server runs *inside* your app.

Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17+ and uses `jakarta.*` packages instead of `javax.*`. Spring Boot 4 keeps the same programming model, so this course applies to both.

steps.title: The smallest app

steps.prompt: `@SpringBootApplication` is a shortcut. Which combination does it stand for?
steps.explanation: It marks the class as a configuration class (via `@SpringBootConfiguration`), turns on auto-configuration and scans for components starting at its own package. It is not a controller, and Boot configures Spring MVC for you, so you rarely write `@EnableWebMvc` yourself.

steps.title: Project layout
steps.body:
Generate projects at **start.spring.io** (or from your IDE): pick Maven or Gradle, a Java version and starters like *Spring Web* and *Spring Data JPA*. You get:

```text
shop/
  mvnw, pom.xml                 (or gradlew, build.gradle.kts)
  src/main/java/com/example/shop/
    ShopApplication.java
    order/OrderController.java
    order/OrderService.java
  src/main/resources/application.properties
  src/test/java/com/example/shop/ShopApplicationTests.java
```

- Keep the main class in the **root package** and everything else in sub-packages: component scanning starts there.
- `./mvnw` (or `./gradlew`) is a wrapper script, so nobody needs to install the build tool.
- Boot manages library versions for you: you add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` without a Hibernate version, and you get one known to work with your Boot version.

steps.title: The controller nobody could find
steps: The `@ComponentScan` inside `@SpringBootApplication` scans `com.example.shop` and everything below it.
`com.example.web` is a *sibling* package, not a sub-package, so `HelloController` is never registered as a bean.
No bean means no mapping for `/hello`, so Spring answers 404. Nothing fails at startup, which is what makes this confusing.
Fix: move the class to `com.example.shop.web` (preferred), or widen the scan with `@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = "com.example")`.
steps.answer: The controller lives outside the scanned package tree. Move it under `com.example.shop`.

steps.prompt: `OrderController` should get a `PriceService` injected, but the app fails at startup. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

Parameter 0 of constructor in OrderController required a bean of type 'PriceService' that could not be found.

Action:

Consider defining a bean of type 'PriceService' in your configuration.
steps.hint: Which packages does `@SpringBootApplication` scan, starting from line 2?
steps.explanation: Component scanning starts at the main class's package, `com.example.shop`, and covers only its sub-packages. `com.example.pricing` is a sibling, so `PriceService` is never registered and the controller's constructor has nothing to receive. Moving it to `com.example.shop.pricing` puts it inside the scanned tree. `@Autowired` doesn't create beans, and `@ComponentScan("com.example.shop")` scans the same tree as before. Moving the controller to `com.example.pricing` only hides the error: the app starts because `OrderController` is no longer scanned either, so its endpoints answer 404.

steps.prompt: You built `shop.jar` from a project with the web starter. What must be installed on the production machine to run it?
choices: A Tomcat server to deploy the jar into
Maven, so it can run `mvn spring-boot:run`
A Spring Boot runtime, installed separately from Java
Just a Java runtime: `java -jar shop.jar` starts the embedded server
steps.explanation: Boot builds an *executable* jar containing your classes, every dependency and the embedded server (Tomcat by default). A Java 17+ runtime is all it needs. Maven is a build tool, not a runtime dependency.

steps.prompt: Your build lists `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` with no version, and Hibernate appears on the classpath anyway. Where does its version come from?
choices: Spring Boot's dependency management, which pins versions that are tested together for your Boot release
The latest Hibernate release, downloaded at build time
Whatever Hibernate version your IDE has cached
The JDK, which ships with a JPA implementation
steps.explanation: Boot's parent POM / Gradle plugin imports a bill of materials (BOM) with compatible versions of hundreds of libraries. Upgrading Boot upgrades them together, which avoids most version-clash headaches. The JDK has no JPA implementation.

steps.prompt: With no configuration at all, which port does the embedded web server listen on?
steps.explanation: The default is **8080**. Change it with `server.port=9090` in `application.properties`, or per environment with the `SERVER_PORT` environment variable (see the configuration lesson).

lessons.title: Beans & dependency injection
lessons.takeaway: Annotate your classes as beans, ask for dependencies through a single constructor with `final` fields, and remember that every bean is one shared instance.

steps.title: Don't new it, ask for it
steps.body:
Without Spring, classes build their own dependencies:

```java
public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentClient payments = new StripePaymentClient(); // hard-wired
}
```

That's hard to test and hard to swap. With **dependency injection**, a class just declares what it needs and someone else supplies it.

In Spring, that someone is the **application context** (the IoC container). It creates your objects, works out what each needs, and passes the pieces in. The objects it manages are called **beans**.

steps.title: Turning classes into beans

steps.prompt: `OrderService` should get the Stripe client injected, but the app fails to start. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

Parameter 0 of constructor in OrderService required a bean of type 'PaymentClient' that could not be found.

Action:

Consider defining a bean of type 'PaymentClient' in your configuration.
fixes: Replace lines 11–15 with field injection: `@Autowired private PaymentClient payments;`
steps.hint: Being on the classpath is not the same as being a bean.
steps.explanation: Spring looked for a bean assignable to `PaymentClient` and found none, because a plain class is invisible to the container. Add `@Component` (or `@Service`) to `StripePaymentClient`, or create it in a `@Bean` method. Injecting by interface is the normal, preferred style, and a single constructor needs no `@Autowired`.

steps.title: Why constructor injection
@Bean for classes you don't own
One instance for everyone
steps: There is exactly one `CheckoutService`, and the server handles many requests at once on different threads.
Two concurrent checkouts both read and write the same `runningTotal` field, so one customer can see the other's total.
Fix: keep per-request data in local variables (`var total = BigDecimal.ZERO;`) or parameters. Fields in a singleton should hold only dependencies and immutable settings.
steps.answer: A race condition. Singleton beans must be stateless (or carefully thread-safe).

steps.explanation: All three classes receive the **same** singleton `VisitCounter`. Creating `A` and `B` bumped it to 2, so the controller's call returns 3. This shared-instance behavior is exactly why mutable fields in beans are dangerous.
steps.hint: How many `VisitCounter` objects does Spring create?

steps.explanation: `@Service` is the idiomatic choice for business logic. `@Component` works identically; `@Service` just tells readers what the class is for.

lessons.title: Auto-configuration: the magic, explained
lessons.takeaway: Auto-configuration is just conditional `@Bean` definitions: they react to your classpath and properties, back off when you define your own bean, and `debug=true` shows every decision.

steps.title: Where do the beans come from?
steps.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` and a Postgres driver, set a URL, and you suddenly have a `DataSource`, a connection pool, an `EntityManagerFactory` and transaction management, without writing any configuration. Who made them?

Spring Boot ships many **auto-configuration classes**: ordinary configuration classes full of `@Bean` methods, listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` inside the Boot jars. `@EnableAutoConfiguration` loads them all, but each is guarded by **conditions**, so only the relevant ones create beans.

steps.title: Conditions

steps.prompt: You declare your own `DataSource` bean in a `@Configuration` class. What happens to the one Boot would auto-configure?
choices: Startup fails because there are now two `DataSource` beans
Boot's bean replaces yours, because auto-configuration runs last
It backs off: `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` sees your bean and skips creating Boot's
Both exist, and Spring picks one at random for each injection point
steps.explanation: Auto-configurations are processed *after* your own configuration, precisely so conditions like `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` can see your beans. Your bean always wins and Boot's default steps aside. That is the main override mechanism.

steps.title: Tune with properties first
steps.body:
Usually you don't replace auto-configured beans, you **tune** them. Each auto-configuration reads a family of properties:

```properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop
server.port=9090
```

When you want different behavior, try in this order:

- Set a property (your IDE autocompletes them; the reference docs list them all).
- Define your own bean of that type to replace Boot's.
- Exclude an auto-configuration completely: `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = SomeAutoConfiguration.class)` or the `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` property.

steps.title: Reading the condition report
steps.problem:
Your app has no `DataSource` bean and you can't see why. You add `debug=true` to `application.properties` (or start with `--debug`) and the log shows a report like this (abridged):

```text
CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT

Positive matches:
   WebMvcAutoConfiguration matched ...

Negative matches:
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class '...EmbeddedDatabaseType'
```

What's going on?
steps: **Positive matches** are auto-configurations whose conditions passed (they created beans). **Negative matches** were skipped, each with the reason.
`DataSourceAutoConfiguration` was skipped because a class from Spring JDBC isn't on the classpath.
So no JDBC or JPA starter made it into the build: the dependency is missing, misspelled, or in the wrong scope.
Fix: add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` (or `spring-boot-starter-jdbc`) plus a database driver. The condition flips to a positive match and the `DataSource` appears.
steps.answer: The JDBC classes are missing from the classpath, so Boot never tried to create a `DataSource`. Add the data starter.

steps.prompt: Which property, set to `true` in `application.properties`, prints the condition evaluation report at startup?
steps.explanation: `debug=true` (or the `--debug` command-line flag) makes Boot log which auto-configurations matched and why the others did not. With Actuator, the `/actuator/conditions` endpoint shows the same report on a running app.

steps.prompt: The app should listen on port 9090. This is its `application.properties`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'
steps.hint: Is `spring.server.port` a key that Boot actually reads?
steps.explanation: The web server's port is `server.port`, not `spring.server.port`. Boot doesn't complain about keys it doesn't know: it simply never reads them, so the server falls back to the default 8080. Switching the separator to `:` keeps the same unknown key, and `debug=true` only prints the condition report. When a setting seems to do nothing, check the exact key with your IDE's autocompletion or the reference docs.

steps.prompt: You add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` to a new project, but no database driver and no `spring.datasource.url`. What happens at startup?
choices: Startup fails: Boot tries to configure a `DataSource` but has no URL and no embedded database to fall back on
It starts, and JPA silently stays disabled
Boot downloads an H2 driver automatically
It starts with an in-memory database created by Hibernate
steps.explanation: The JPA starter puts the `DataSource` classes on the classpath, so the condition matches and Boot tries to build one. With an embedded database such as H2 on the classpath it would create an in-memory database; with neither a driver nor a URL it fails with a "Failed to configure a DataSource" message. Add a driver and URL (or H2 for local work).
steps.hint: Which condition does the starter satisfy?

steps.prompt: Your app uses the web starter and you never declared anything about JSON, yet controllers return JSON. Which explanation is right?
choices: The JDK has a built-in JSON serializer that Spring MVC uses
`@SpringBootApplication` scans the Jackson jar for `@Component` classes
An auto-configuration conditioned on Jackson being on the classpath created a JSON mapper and plugged it into Spring MVC
steps.explanation: The web starter brings Jackson, and Jackson on the classpath satisfies `@ConditionalOnClass` checks in Boot's auto-configuration, which registers a mapper and wires it into Spring MVC's message converters. Component scanning only covers your own packages, never library jars.

lessons.title: When wiring fails: duplicate beans & cycles
lessons.takeaway: Two beans of one type need `@Primary` or `@Qualifier` (or inject them all as a `List`); a dependency cycle needs a redesign, not a workaround.

steps.title: Two candidates, one slot
Three ways to choose

steps.prompt: Orders should be charged through Stripe. PayPal is used elsewhere, so both clients must stay beans. The app fails at startup. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

Parameter 0 of constructor in com.example.shop.OrderService required a single bean, but 2 were found:
	- paypalClient: defined in file [  ...]
	- stripeClient: defined in file [  ...]
  ...

Action:

Consider marking one of the beans as @Primary, updating the consumer to accept multiple beans, or using @Qualifier to identify the bean that should be consumed
fixes: Change line 11 to `public OrderService(@Qualifier("stripeClient") PaymentClient payments) {`
Change line 11 to `public OrderService(@Qualifier("StripeClient") PaymentClient payments) {`
Add `@Primary` above line 1 and above line 4
steps.hint: The error lists the two candidates by bean name. Which line has to say which one it wants?
steps.explanation: The constructor asks for *a* `PaymentClient` and two beans match, so Spring refuses to guess. `@Qualifier("stripeClient")` names the one it wants, using the default bean name: the class name with a lowercase first letter, exactly as the error lists it. `@Autowired` only says "inject this", which the single constructor already does, so the same error comes back. `"StripeClient"` with a capital S matches no bean, so startup fails with *No qualifying bean*. And `@Primary` on **both** fails with *more than one 'primary' bean found*; on `StripeClient` alone it would work too.

steps.title: Circular dependencies
Breaking a cycle
steps.problem: `OrderService` calls `invoices.createFor(order)`, and `InvoiceService` calls `orders.totalOf(orderId)` to compute the invoice amount. How do you break the cycle?
steps: Ask what each side really needs. `InvoiceService` doesn't need all of `OrderService`, only an order's total.
Extract that into its own bean, e.g. `OrderPricing` with `totalOf(orderId)`, which depends only on `OrderRepository`.
Now the arrows run one way: `OrderService` → `InvoiceService` → `OrderPricing` → `OrderRepository`. No loop.
Bonus: each class got smaller and easier to unit-test.
steps.answer: Extract the shared piece into a third bean so dependencies form a straight line.

steps.prompt: `StripeClient` is marked `@Primary`. `RefundService`'s constructor parameter is `@Qualifier("paypalClient") PaymentClient payments`. What gets injected into `RefundService`?
choices: `PaypalClient`, because the explicit qualifier narrows the choice first
steps.explanation: `@Primary` is only a tie-breaker for injection points that don't say which bean they want. An explicit `@Qualifier` selects the bean by name, so `PaypalClient` is injected. Everywhere else, `StripeClient` stays the default.

steps.prompt: All beans below use constructor injection. Which setup makes the app fail at startup?
choices: `A` needs a `List<Handler>` and there are three `Handler` beans
steps.hint: Draw the arrows and look for a loop.
steps.explanation: `A → B → C → A` is a cycle: no bean can be built first. Chains and shared dependencies are fine (Spring builds `C` once and shares it), and a `List<Handler>` simply receives all matching beans.

steps.prompt: Which annotation, placed on one of several implementations, makes it the default choice wherever an injection point is ambiguous?
steps.explanation: `@Primary` marks the preferred candidate. Injection points that need a different one can still ask for it explicitly with `@Qualifier`.

units.title: Building a REST API
units.description: Controllers, JSON, status codes, validation and clean error responses: the daily work of a Spring Boot back end.

lessons.title: REST controllers: requests in, JSON out
lessons.takeaway: `@RestController` methods map requests with `@GetMapping`/`@PostMapping`, read input via `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam` and `@RequestBody`, and return records as JSON, or a `ResponseEntity` when the status code matters.

steps.title: A JSON endpoint
Three ways to read input
Records as DTOs
steps.body:
Use **records** for request and response bodies. Jackson reads and writes them out of the box:

```java
public record CreateBookRequest(String title, String author, int year) {}
public record BookResponse(Long id, String title, String author) {}
```

A `BookResponse` is sent as `{"id":42,"title":"Dune","author":"Herbert"}`.

Keep these DTOs separate from your database entities: you control exactly what goes over the wire (no leaked `passwordHash` field), and you can change the database without breaking clients.

choices: 400 Bad Request: the required parameter is missing
steps.explanation: `@RequestParam` is required by default, so Spring rejects the request before your method runs (a `MissingServletRequestParameterException`, mapped to 400). Make it optional with `required = false`, a `defaultValue`, or an `Optional<String>` parameter. The path itself matched, so it is not a 404.

steps.prompt: `POST /api/books` with the body `{"title":"Dune","author":"Herbert"}` should answer with that book as JSON (`BookResponse` is the record from above). Click the line with the bug.
fixes: Change line 8 to `public BookResponse create(@RequestBody CreateBookRequest req) {`
Change line 8 to `public BookResponse create(@RequestParam CreateBookRequest req) {`
steps.hint: Which annotation tells Spring to read the JSON body into a parameter?
steps.explanation: Without `@RequestBody`, Spring never reads the body: it tries to fill the record from query parameters and form fields, finds none, and passes in a request whose fields are all `null`. Your method happily returns 200. `@RequestBody` hands the JSON to Jackson instead. `@ResponseBody` is about the *return* value (and `@RestController` already adds it), `consumes` only restricts which requests match, and `@RequestParam` looks for a `?req=` query parameter, so the request fails with 400.

items: Jackson reads the JSON body into a `CreateBookRequest`
Jackson writes the `BookResponse` into the response body as JSON
The client receives `200 OK` and the book as JSON
steps.hint: A method can't run until its arguments exist, and there's nothing to send back until it returns.
steps.explanation: Spring first finds the handler: the class prefix `/api/books` plus `@PostMapping` matches the path and the HTTP method. Your method can't run until its argument exists, so `@RequestBody` hands the JSON to Jackson to build the record first (if the JSON can't be read, the client gets 400 and your method never runs). Then your code runs like any Java method. `@RestController` includes `@ResponseBody`, so the returned record is written as JSON, and because you returned a plain object, the status is 200.

steps.title: Status codes with ResponseEntity
Not found, the clean way
steps.problem: `GET /api/books/99` asks for a book that doesn't exist. `books.findById(id)` returns `Optional<BookResponse>`. Respond 200 with the book, or 404.
steps: Returning `books.findById(id).orElse(null)` gives **200 with an empty body**: it claims success, which misleads clients.
Present → `ResponseEntity.ok(book)` → 200 with JSON. Empty → 404 with no body. (`ResponseEntity.of(optional)` is a built-in shortcut for exactly this.)
In a bigger app you'd rather throw a `BookNotFoundException` from the service and map it to 404 in one place. That's the error-handling lesson.

steps.explanation: Spring doesn't infer 201 from `@PostMapping`: a returned object means 200. For a proper REST create, return `ResponseEntity.created(location).body(saved)` or add `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)`.
A plain `@Controller` treats return values as view names. `@RestController` adds `@ResponseBody` to every method, so return values are serialized (to JSON) into the response body.

lessons.title: Validating input
lessons.takeaway: Put Jakarta Bean Validation constraints on your request records and `@Valid` on the `@RequestBody`; bad input becomes a 400 before your code runs.

steps.title: Never trust the body
The constraints you'll actually use
steps.body:
- `@NotNull`: not null (but `""` passes).
- `@NotEmpty`: not null and length > 0 (but `"   "` passes).
- `@NotBlank`: contains at least one non-whitespace character. The usual choice for strings.
- `@Size(min = .., max = ..)`: string length or collection size.
- `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Positive`: numbers.
- `@Email`, `@Pattern(regexp = "...")`: formats.
- `@Past`, `@Future`: dates.

Most constraints treat `null` as valid, so add `@NotNull` when a value is required: `@NotNull @Positive Integer quantity`.

steps.prompt: A field is annotated `@NotEmpty String name`, and the controller uses `@Valid`. A client sends `{"name": "   "}`. What happens?
choices: 400, but only if the record is also annotated with `@Valid`
steps.explanation: `@NotEmpty` only checks that the string is non-null with length > 0, and `"   "` has length 3. To reject whitespace-only strings, use `@NotBlank`.

steps.prompt: Every order line needs a quantity of at least 1, so posting `{"product": "pen"}` (no quantity) should get 400. Click the line with the bug.
steps.hint: What does `@Positive` say about `null`?
steps.explanation: Like most constraints, `@Positive` treats `null` as valid: it only checks values that are present. A missing quantity is `null`, so validation passes. Adding `@NotNull` makes the field required, while `@Positive` still rejects 0 and negatives. `@Min(1)` has the same blind spot for `null`. `@NotEmpty` is for strings and collections: on an `Integer` it throws `UnexpectedTypeException`, a 500 on every request. `@Valid` cascades into nested objects and does nothing for a number.

steps.title: The forgotten @Valid
steps: Constraint annotations are just metadata. Something has to *trigger* validation.
For a request body, the trigger is `@Valid` (or Spring's `@Validated`) on the parameter. Without it, Spring deserializes the JSON and calls your method as-is.
Second suspect, for when `@Valid` *is* present but nothing happens: the validation starter is missing, so there is no validator to run the rules.
Fix: `create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest req)`. The same request now gets 400 listing three field errors.

steps.prompt: With `@Valid` in place, a client sends `{"name": "Ann", "email": "ann@example.com", "age": 12}`, where `age` has `@Min(18)`. What does the client get by default?
steps.explanation: The failed constraint raises `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which Spring MVC maps to **400**. Some teams prefer 422; you can choose that yourself in an exception handler (next lesson). `@Min` is for numbers.

steps.title: Nested objects and business rules

steps.prompt: `OrderRequest` has `@NotNull Address shipping` (no `@Valid` on that field), and `Address` has `@NotBlank String city`. The controller uses `@Valid @RequestBody`. A request arrives with `"shipping": {"city": ""}`. What happens?
choices: Validation passes: `Address`'s constraints aren't checked without `@Valid` on the field
steps.hint: Which object does `@Valid` on the parameter actually validate?
steps.explanation: `@Valid` on the parameter validates `OrderRequest` itself: `shipping` is not null, so that passes. Without `@Valid` on the `shipping` field, validation doesn't cascade into `Address`, so the blank city slips through.

steps.prompt:
Fill in the constraint that rejects `null`, `""` and `"   "`:

```java
public record Tag(@___ String label) {}
```
steps.explanation: `@NotBlank` (from `jakarta.validation.constraints`) requires at least one non-whitespace character, which also rules out null and the empty string.

lessons.title: Error handling with ProblemDetail
lessons.takeaway: Throw meaningful exceptions from your services and translate them to status codes in one `@RestControllerAdvice` that returns `ProblemDetail` bodies.

steps.title: What happens by default
steps.body:
If a controller method throws and nothing handles the exception, Spring Boot's error handling answers **500 Internal Server Error** with a small JSON body (timestamp, status, error, path).

Spring MVC already maps its own exceptions sensibly:

- failed `@Valid` body, malformed JSON, missing `@RequestParam`, wrong type in a path variable → **400**
- no matching path → **404**; wrong HTTP method → **405**; unsupported `Content-Type` → **415**

But your `BookNotFoundException` is just another `RuntimeException` to Spring: **500**. That's wrong, because the client asked for something missing; the server didn't crash.

steps.title: One place for all mappings
What the client sees
steps.problem: `BookService.find(99)` throws `new BookNotFoundException("Book 99 not found")`. With the advice above in place, what does `GET /api/books/99` return?
steps: The exception escapes the controller, and Spring looks for a matching `@ExceptionHandler`. It finds `notFound` in the advice.
The handler builds a `ProblemDetail` with status 404 and the message as its `detail`.

Spring sends status **404** with `Content-Type: application/problem+json` and a body like:

```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "Book 99 not found",
  "instance": "/api/books/99"
}
```
Every error in your API now has the same, machine-readable shape, which clients can parse in one place.
steps.answer: 404 with a `problem+json` body describing the error.

steps.prompt: There is **no** `@RestControllerAdvice`. `BookService` throws `BookNotFoundException extends RuntimeException`. What status does the client get?
steps.explanation: Spring knows nothing about your exception, so an unhandled one is a 500. To get 404: map it in an `@ExceptionHandler`, annotate the exception class with `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)`, or throw `ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ...)`.

steps.prompt: `books.findById(id)` returns an `Optional<BookResponse>`. With this advice in place, `GET /api/books/99` (no such book) should return 404 with a `ProblemDetail`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
500 Internal Server Error
{"timestamp":"…","status":500,"error":"Internal Server Error","path":"/api/books/99"}

Server log:
java.util.NoSuchElementException: No value present
  ...
fixes: Change line 4 to `return books.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new BookNotFoundException("Book " + id + " not found"));`
Change line 4 to `return books.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("Book " + id + " not found"));`
steps.hint: Which exception does `orElseThrow()` with no arguments throw? Which one does the handler catch?
steps.explanation: `orElseThrow()` without arguments throws `NoSuchElementException`. The advice only handles `BookNotFoundException`, so no handler matches and Spring answers 500. Throwing the exception the handler expects routes it to `notFound`, which builds the 404 `ProblemDetail`. `orElse(null)` gives 200 with an empty body, a plain `RuntimeException` still matches no handler, and `@ResponseStatus` on the controller method sets the status of *successful* responses (book 42 would come back as 404) while the missing book still gets 500.

steps.title: Other options & good practice
steps.body:
- `throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Book not found")`: quick and needs no custom class, but HTTP details leak into your service layer.
- `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)` on your exception class: a fixed status, very little code.
- Want `ProblemDetail` bodies for Spring MVC's built-in errors too (validation, malformed JSON)? Set `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`, or have your advice extend `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`.

Whatever you choose: never send stack traces or SQL messages to clients, and log unexpected 500s on the server.

steps.prompt: One advice has two handlers: `@ExceptionHandler(RuntimeException.class)` returning 500, and `@ExceptionHandler(BookNotFoundException.class)` returning 404. A `BookNotFoundException` (a subclass of `RuntimeException`) is thrown. Which handler runs?
choices: The `BookNotFoundException` handler: the closest match in the exception hierarchy wins
The `RuntimeException` handler, if it is declared first in the class
Neither: startup fails because both handlers match
steps.explanation: Spring picks the handler whose declared exception type is nearest to the thrown exception's class, so the specific handler wins and the generic one becomes a catch-all for everything else. Declaration order doesn't matter.

steps.prompt: Your API style guide says invalid request bodies must return **422** instead of 400. What do you add?
choices: An `@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)` in your advice that returns a `ProblemDetail` with status 422
steps.hint: Which exception does a failed `@Valid` raise?
steps.explanation: Validation failures surface as `MethodArgumentNotValidException`. Handling it yourself lets you pick the status and include the field errors (from `ex.getBindingResult()`) in the body. The other options don't exist or don't apply to DTOs.
`@RestControllerAdvice` = `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody`. It is the standard home for API-wide exception mappings.

units.title: Data & configuration
units.description: Persist entities with Spring Data JPA and configure one build for every environment.

lessons.title: Spring Data JPA: entities & repositories
lessons.takeaway: Map a class with `@Entity`, extend `JpaRepository<Entity, Id>`, let method names like `findByEmail` become queries, and switch to `@Query` when the names get long.

steps.title: An entity
A repository with zero code

steps.prompt: `CustomerRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long>` should save customers with a generated id, but the app fails at startup. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'entityManagerFactory' ...
  ...
Caused by: org.hibernate.AnnotationException: Entity 'com.example.shop.Customer' has no identifier (every '@Entity' class must declare or inherit at least one '@Id' or '@EmbeddedId' property)
steps.hint: `@GeneratedValue` says how to fill in the key. Which annotation says which field *is* the key?
steps.explanation: Every entity needs a primary key marked with `@Id`. `@GeneratedValue` only describes how the id is generated; it doesn't make the field the identifier, so Hibernate rejects the class while building the `EntityManagerFactory`. Changing the strategy or renaming the field still leaves the class without an `@Id`. Putting `@Id` on `email` fails too: Hibernate then complains that `id` has `@GeneratedValue` but is not part of an identifier.

steps.prompt: You add `Optional<Customer> findByEmial(String email);` to the repository (note the typo). What happens?
choices: The app fails to start: Spring Data finds no property `emial` on `Customer`
It compiles, and the method always returns an empty `Optional`
It throws a `NullPointerException` the first time it's called
steps.explanation: Derived query names are parsed when the repository bean is created at startup, so a misspelled property fails fast with an error like *No property 'emial' found for type 'Customer'*. Better a startup failure than a silent bug.

steps.prompt:
`Customer` has a field `LocalDate signupDate`. Write the derived method name that returns customers who signed up **after** a given date:

```java
List<Customer> ___(LocalDate date);
```
steps.hint: `findBy` + property name (capitalized) + a comparison keyword.
steps.explanation: `findBySignupDateAfter` becomes `... where c.signupDate > ?1`. `GreaterThan` works too; `After`/`Before` simply read better for dates.

steps.title: @Query when names get silly
Schema and transactions: the basics
steps.body:
- **Schema**: `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` defaults to `create-drop` for an embedded database like H2 (when no migration tool is present) and to `none` otherwise. In production, manage the schema with Flyway or Liquibase and keep `ddl-auto` at `validate` or `none`.
- **Transactions**: built-in repository methods such as `save` already run in their own transaction. When one service method makes **several** changes that must succeed or fail together, annotate it with `@Transactional`; a `RuntimeException` rolls all of them back.
- In development, `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` prints the SQL Hibernate runs.

steps.title: Registering a customer
steps.problem: Write a service method that registers a customer and rejects duplicate emails with a `DuplicateEmailException` (a `RuntimeException` you map to 409 Conflict).
steps: Inject the repository through the constructor: `public CustomerService(CustomerRepository customers)`.
Check the business rule first with the derived query: `if (customers.existsByEmail(req.email())) throw new DuplicateEmailException(req.email());`.
Create and save the entity: `Customer saved = customers.save(new Customer(req.email(), req.name()));`. `save` returns the entity with its generated `id`.
Map the entity to a DTO before returning it: `return new CustomerResponse(saved.getId(), saved.getEmail(), saved.getName());`.
Keep the `unique = true` column constraint too: two simultaneous requests can both pass the `exists` check, and the database is the final guard.
steps.answer: Check `existsByEmail`, then `save`, then map to a response record; let the unique constraint catch races.

steps.prompt: An app uses PostgreSQL, has no `ddl-auto` setting and no Flyway or Liquibase. You add a new `@Entity` and start the app. What does Hibernate do to the schema?
choices: Nothing: for a non-embedded database the default is `none`, so the table must already exist
Fails startup, because `ddl-auto` must always be set
steps.explanation: Boot only defaults to `create-drop` for embedded databases such as H2. For a real database it defaults to `none`, so queries against the new entity fail until a migration creates the table. That is deliberate: schema changes in production should be explicit, reviewed migrations.

lessons.title: Configuration, profiles & environment overrides
lessons.takeaway: Put defaults in `application.properties`, bind groups of settings to a `@ConfigurationProperties` record, and override per environment with profiles and environment variables, never by rebuilding.

steps.title: application.properties (or .yml)
steps.body:
```properties
server.port=8081
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
app.mail.host=smtp.example.com
app.mail.port=587
app.mail.timeout=5s
```

The same in `application.yml`:

```yaml
app:
  mail:
    host: smtp.example.com
    port: 587
    timeout: 5s
```

Boot's own keys (`server.*`, `spring.*`, `management.*`) tune auto-configuration. Your own keys (here `app.*`) are for your code. Pick one format per project.

steps.title: Typed settings with @ConfigurationProperties
Profiles
steps.body:
A **profile** is a named set of overrides. Boot loads `application.properties`, then `application-{profile}.properties` for each active profile, whose values win:

```properties
# application-dev.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:shop
logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
```

```properties
# application-prod.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/shop
```

Activate one with `spring.profiles.active=prod`, for example via the environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`. Beans can be profile-specific too: `@Profile("dev")` on a class or `@Bean` method.

steps.title: Who wins? Environment variables & relaxed binding
steps.body:
Simplified precedence, highest first:

- Command-line arguments: `java -jar app.jar --server.port=9000`
- OS environment variables
- `application-{profile}.properties`
- `application.properties`

Environment variables use **relaxed binding**: uppercase, dots become underscores, dashes are dropped. `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` sets `spring.datasource.url`; `APP_MAIL_HOST` sets `app.mail.host`.

That's how containers and cloud platforms inject settings and secrets: the jar is identical everywhere, only the environment changes.

steps.title: Tracing one setting
steps.problem: `application.properties` has `app.mail.port=25`, `application-prod.properties` has `app.mail.port=587`, and the container sets `APP_MAIL_PORT=2525`. The app runs with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`. What does `MailProperties.port()` return?
steps: Start at the bottom: `application.properties` says 25.
The `prod` profile is active, so `application-prod.properties` overrides it: 587.
`APP_MAIL_PORT` maps to `app.mail.port` through relaxed binding, and environment variables beat config files: 2525.

steps.prompt: Same files and `APP_MAIL_PORT=2525` as above, but now the app is started with `java -jar shop.jar --app.mail.port=465`. Which port does `MailProperties.port()` return?
steps.explanation: Command-line arguments sit above environment variables, which sit above every config file. 465 wins. That makes `--key=value` handy for one-off overrides.

steps.prompt: In production you want to set `spring.datasource.password` through an environment variable. What is the variable called?
steps.explanation: Uppercase it and replace the dots with underscores: `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD`. Secrets belong in the environment (or a secret store), never in a committed properties file.

steps.prompt: You run the app locally without activating any profile. The project has `application.properties` and `application-dev.properties`. Which values apply?
choices: Both files: `dev` is the default profile
Only `application.properties`; the dev values apply only when `dev` is active
None: startup fails without an active profile
steps.explanation: With no profile set, Spring activates a profile literally named `default`, so it would load `application-default.properties` if that existed, but never the `dev` file. Activate `dev` explicitly, e.g. with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev` or in your IDE run configuration.

steps.prompt: This `application.yml` feeds `MailProperties` from above (`prefix = "app.mail"`). At startup the app prints the record, which should show `timeout=PT5S` (5 seconds). Click the line with the bug.
steps.code:
server:
  port: 8081
app:
  mail:
    host: smtp.example.com
    port: 587
  timeout: 5s
fixes: Indent line 7 by two more spaces, so `timeout` sits under `mail:`
steps.hint: In YAML, indentation decides the full key. What is line 7's full key?
steps.explanation: YAML builds keys from indentation. Line 7 is indented like `mail:`, so it is a sibling of `mail` and becomes `app.timeout`, which `MailProperties` (bound to `app.mail`) never reads: the field stays `null` and nothing complains. Indented under `mail:`, it becomes `app.mail.timeout` and binds as 5 seconds. Changing the value's format doesn't change the key, and `mail-timeout` becomes `app.mail-timeout`, still outside `app.mail`.

lessons.title: Transactions & the N+1 problem
lessons.takeaway: `@Transactional` works through a proxy, so self-calls and checked exceptions surprise people; and lazy associations touched in a loop silently turn 1 query into N+1.

steps.title: How @Transactional really works
steps.body:
Spring wraps your bean in a **proxy**. A call from *another* bean goes through the proxy, which starts a transaction, calls your method, then commits, or rolls back if it threw. Consequences:

- **Self-invocation**: calling `this.rebuild()` from inside the same class skips the proxy, so `@Transactional` on `rebuild` is ignored for that call.
- **Rollback rules**: by default only unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException`, `Error`) roll back. A checked exception **commits**. Use `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)` to change that.
- **Dirty checking**: inside a transaction, changes to entities you loaded are written at commit, even without calling `save()`.

choices: Rolled back: any exception rolls the transaction back
Rolled back, but only if `accounts` is a `@Repository`
The transaction stays open until the next request
Committed: checked exceptions don't trigger a rollback by default
steps.explanation: Spring's default rule is "roll back on unchecked exceptions only". The debit is committed while the credit never happens: money disappears. Use `@Transactional(rollbackFor = InsufficientFundsException.class)` or make the exception unchecked.
steps.hint: The default rollback rule is about the *kind* of exception.

choices: No: the internal call doesn't pass through the proxy, so the annotation has no effect
Yes: the annotation is on the method being executed
Only if the class is also annotated with `@Repository`
steps.explanation: `rebuild()` is called on `this`, the raw object, not on the proxy that other beans see. Fixes: put `@Transactional` on `nightly()`, or move `rebuild()` into another bean.

steps.prompt:
Each method below saves an order, then ends as described. The call comes from another bean, through the proxy. When the call is over, is the saved order undone or kept?

(`InsufficientFundsException extends Exception`; `PaymentDeclinedException extends RuntimeException`.)

items.text: `@Transactional`, catches its own `IllegalStateException` and returns normally
Not annotated: calls `this.rebuild()`, a `@Transactional` method that saves, then throws `IllegalStateException`

steps.hint: Ask two questions: did an exception actually leave the proxy, and is it unchecked (`RuntimeException` or `Error`) or listed in `rollbackFor`?
steps.explanation: By default the proxy rolls back only when an **unchecked** exception (`RuntimeException` or `Error`, including your own subclasses) escapes the method; `rollbackFor` adds others. Checked exceptions like `IOException` or a custom `extends Exception` **commit** the half-finished work. If the method catches the exception itself, the proxy sees a normal return and commits. And `this.rebuild()` bypasses the proxy, so there is no transaction at all: the save commits on its own before the exception is thrown.

steps.title: The N+1 problem

steps.prompt: With the loop above and **40** authors in the database, how many SQL queries run in total?
steps.explanation: One query loads the 40 authors, then each author's lazy `books` collection costs one more: 1 + 40 = **41**. Hence the name N+1.

steps.title: Fixing it
Saved without save()
steps: `findById` loads `c` into the persistence context, which now tracks it as a *managed* entity.
`setName` changes it in memory; Hibernate still knows the original state.
At commit, Hibernate compares the two (dirty checking) and issues an `UPDATE` for the changed column.
Without the surrounding transaction nothing would flush that change, so you would need an explicit `customers.save(c)`.
steps.answer: Yes: dirty checking writes the change when the transaction commits.

units.title: Testing & production
units.description: Fast, focused tests with Spring's test slices, then the extras that get an app safely into production.

lessons.title: Testing: slices, MockMvc & @MockitoBean
lessons.takeaway: Unit-test services with plain JUnit and Mockito, use `@WebMvcTest` or `@DataJpaTest` to test one layer in a small context, and keep `@SpringBootTest` for a few end-to-end checks.

steps.title: Pick the smallest test that works
steps.body:
`spring-boot-starter-test` brings JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ and Spring's test support. Three levels:

- **Plain unit test**: `new OrderService(mockRepo)`, no Spring at all. Milliseconds, and possible thanks to constructor injection (see the Unit Testing course).
- **Slice test**: starts one layer only. `@WebMvcTest` (controllers, JSON, validation, advice) or `@DataJpaTest` (entities, repositories, a test database).
- **`@SpringBootTest`**: the whole application context. Most realistic, slowest.

Slices are faster because they load a fraction of the beans and auto-configurations. Spring caches contexts between test classes, but each distinct setup (a different set of mocks, say) means another context to start.

steps.title: @WebMvcTest + MockMvc

steps.prompt: A `@WebMvcTest(BookController.class)` test fails while loading the context: *No qualifying bean of type 'BookService' available*. Why?
choices: MockMvc can only test controllers that have no dependencies
`@WebMvcTest` doesn't create `@Service` beans, so the controller's dependency must be supplied, typically with `@MockitoBean`
The test class must also be annotated with `@SpringBootApplication`
steps.explanation: The web slice only includes web-layer components (controllers, advice, converters, filters). Services and repositories are left out on purpose, so you provide them: usually `@MockitoBean BookService books;`, or `@Import` the real class if you really want it.

steps.title: Testing validation and errors
steps.problem: Write a test proving that posting a book with a blank title returns 400 **and** never reaches the service.
steps:
Send a body that breaks `@NotBlank title`:

```java
mvc.perform(post("/api/books")
        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
        .content("""
            {"title": "", "author": "Herbert", "year": 1965}
            """))
   .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());
```
`@WebMvcTest` includes validation and your `@RestControllerAdvice`, so this runs the real 400 path, including your error body.
Then check the mock was never touched: `verify(books, never()).create(any());`.
That's the sweet spot for slice tests: routing, JSON, validation and error mapping, all without a database.

steps.title: @DataJpaTest and @SpringBootTest

steps.prompt: You want to check that a custom repository query, `findTop5ByOrderByCreatedAtDesc`, returns the right rows. Which setup fits best?
choices: A plain Mockito test that mocks the repository
steps.explanation: Only a real database run can tell you whether the query is right, and `@DataJpaTest` gives you that with the smallest context. Mocking the repository tests nothing about the query, and a full `@SpringBootTest` is slower than it needs to be.

steps.prompt: You want to verify that `DELETE /api/books/7` answers 204 and calls `books.delete(7L)`. Which setup fits best?
choices: A plain unit test that calls `controller.delete(7L)` directly
steps.hint: The question is about HTTP behavior, not about the database.
steps.explanation: The web slice exercises the real routing and status mapping through MockMvc, while the mocked service lets you `verify(books).delete(7L)`. Calling the method directly skips routing; a full context with a database adds cost without testing anything extra.
`@MockitoBean` is the current annotation. You will still see `@MockBean` in older code; it was deprecated in Spring Boot 3.4 in favor of `@MockitoBean`.

steps.prompt: This web-slice test should pass, with a fake `BookService` behind the controller. Instead the context fails to load. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

Parameter 0 of constructor in BookController required a bean of type 'BookService' that could not be found.
  ...
BookControllerTest.returnsBook » IllegalState Failed to load ApplicationContext
steps.hint: `@Mock` creates a mock inside the test class. Does the Spring context ever see it?
steps.explanation: `@Mock` is plain Mockito: it makes a mock for the test object (and only with Mockito's JUnit extension), but never registers it in the Spring context. `@WebMvcTest` leaves `@Service` beans out, so `BookController` still has no `BookService` to receive. `@MockitoBean` puts the mock into the context as the `BookService` bean and also injects it into your field for `when(...)`. `@Autowired` asks for a bean that doesn't exist, `@Spy` has the same problem as `@Mock`, and `@WebMvcTest` without a class loads every controller but still no services.

lessons.title: Spring Security basics
lessons.takeaway: Adding Spring Security locks every endpoint by default; open things up deliberately in a `SecurityFilterChain` bean, specific rules first and `anyRequest()` last.

steps.title: Secure by default
steps.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-security` and restart. Without writing any code:

- **Every** endpoint now requires authentication.
- Boot creates a single user named `user` with a random password printed in the startup log. That's for development only.
- Unauthenticated API calls get **401 Unauthorized**; browsers are redirected to a generated login page.
- CSRF protection is on, so state-changing requests (`POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) without a CSRF token are rejected with **403**.

steps.prompt: You add `spring-boot-starter-security` to the book API and change nothing else. What does an anonymous `GET /api/books` from curl return now?
choices: 200: GET requests stay public by default
404: controllers are disabled until you configure security
steps.explanation: Once Spring Security is on the classpath, Boot's default configuration requires authentication for every request. No credentials means 401. Nothing is public until you say so.

steps.title: Your own rules: SecurityFilterChain

steps.prompt:
What happens with this configuration?

```java
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
    .anyRequest().authenticated()
    .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll())
```
choices: Public paths still require login, because the first rule matches everything
Only GET requests to the public paths are allowed anonymously
The app fails to start: no rule may be added after `anyRequest()`
steps.hint: Spring Security checks the rule list while it is being built.
steps.explanation: `anyRequest()` has to be the final rule; Spring Security rejects any `requestMatchers` added after it with an error at startup. Put the specific `permitAll()` rules first and `anyRequest().authenticated()` last.

steps.title: 401 vs 403, and CSRF
steps.body:
- **401 Unauthorized** really means *unauthenticated*: we don't know who you are (missing or bad credentials).
- **403 Forbidden** means we know who you are, but you're not allowed: a missing role, or a failed check such as CSRF.

CSRF protection defends browser sessions that rely on cookies. A stateless API that authenticates every request with a header (`Authorization: Bearer ...`) isn't exposed the same way, which is why such APIs commonly turn it off with `http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())`. Keep it on for cookie-based logins.

steps.prompt: Using the `SecurityConfig` above (with CSRF disabled), user `ann`, who has only the `USER` role, sends `DELETE /api/books/3` with valid credentials. What is the response?
steps.explanation: Ann is authenticated, so it isn't a 401, but the matching rule requires role `ADMIN`. Authenticated-but-not-allowed is **403**.

steps.prompt: Using the `SecurityConfig` above with CSRF disabled, users `ann` (role `USER`) and `max` (role `ADMIN`), and the actuator health endpoint on the classpath, what does each request get?
steps.hint: First ask: do we know who this is? Only then ask: are they allowed?
steps.explanation: The first matching rule decides. Public paths and health are `permitAll()`, so anyone gets through. Everything else needs a known user: no credentials or a wrong password means we don't know who you are, so **401**, even for the `DELETE` that would need `ADMIN` anyway. Once Ann is authenticated, she can `GET` (`authenticated()`), but the `DELETE` rule wants role `ADMIN`: known but not allowed is **403**. Max has `ADMIN`, so his `DELETE` succeeds.

steps.title: The health check that broke
steps.problem: After adding Spring Security, the platform's health probe (`GET /actuator/health`) starts failing and your containers keep restarting. Fix it.
steps: The probe sends no credentials, so it now gets 401, and the platform concludes the app is unhealthy.
Declare a `SecurityFilterChain` bean with `.requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()` placed **before** `.anyRequest().authenticated()`.
Open only the health endpoint. Never make `/actuator/env` or heap dumps public: they can reveal secrets.
Restart: the probe gets 200 with `{"status":"UP"}` again, and everything else still needs a login.
steps.answer: Permit the health endpoint explicitly in your `SecurityFilterChain`, before `anyRequest()`.

steps.prompt:
Fill in the method that lets anyone, logged in or not, reach the matched paths:

```java
.requestMatchers("/api/public/**").___()
```
steps.explanation: `permitAll()` skips the authentication requirement for matching requests. Its counterparts are `authenticated()`, `hasRole("...")` and `denyAll()`.

lessons.title: Actuator & shipping your app
lessons.takeaway: Actuator gives you health checks and metrics for free, and a Boot app ships as one executable jar (or a buildpack-built image) configured by the environment it runs in.

steps.title: Actuator
steps.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` to get production endpoints under `/actuator`:

- `/actuator/health`: `{"status":"UP"}` with HTTP 200, or `DOWN` with **503** when a checked component (database, disk space...) is unhealthy. Load balancers and Kubernetes probes poll this.
- `/actuator/metrics`: Micrometer metrics such as `http.server.requests`, JVM memory and connection-pool usage. Add a registry like Prometheus to export them.
- `info`, `loggers`, `conditions`, `env` and more.

Over HTTP, only `health` is exposed by default. Opt in to others explicitly:

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
```

steps.prompt: The app is running but its database is down. A load balancer polls `/actuator/health`. What does it receive?
choices: 200 with `{"status":"UP"}`: the web server itself is fine
404: the health endpoint disappears when a component fails
steps.explanation: With a `DataSource` present, a database health indicator is included in the overall status. If it fails, the aggregate becomes `DOWN`, which maps to HTTP **503**, so the load balancer can stop routing traffic to this instance.

steps.prompt: After adding Actuator, `/actuator/health` works but `/actuator/metrics` returns 404. Why?
choices: Metrics require a Prometheus server to be running first
Only `health` is exposed over HTTP by default; add `metrics` to `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`
Metrics are only available in the `prod` profile
steps.explanation: Endpoints are opt-in for web exposure because several reveal internals. Security blocking it would give 401/403, not 404. Treat `env`, `heapdump` and similar endpoints as sensitive and never expose them publicly.

steps.prompt: Actuator is on the classpath and Spring Security is not. With the setting shown, what does a plain `GET` to each endpoint return?
steps.hint: `include=...` is short for `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. Out of the box, which single endpoint is exposed over HTTP?
steps.explanation: Over HTTP only `health` is exposed by default; every other endpoint answers 404 until you list it in `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. Listing `health,info,metrics` exposes exactly those three, so `env` stays hidden, and `*` exposes everything that's enabled, `loggers` included. Be careful with `*` in production: it also exposes sensitive endpoints like `env`, so keep those off public networks.

steps.title: Build & run
steps.body:
```bash
./mvnw spring-boot:run                    # run from source while developing
./mvnw clean package                      # build target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
java -jar target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

./gradlew bootRun                         # Gradle equivalents
./gradlew bootJar                         # build/libs/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
```

The jar is **executable**: it holds your classes, every dependency and the embedded server. The same artifact runs in every environment; only profiles, environment variables and command-line arguments change.

steps.title: Container images without a Dockerfile
steps.body:
```bash
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image            # or: ./gradlew bootBuildImage
docker run -p 8080:8080 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod shop:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
```

`build-image` uses **Cloud Native Buildpacks** to produce an OCI image with a suitable JRE, sensible memory settings and dependencies in separate layers, so rebuilding after a code change only replaces a small layer. It needs a local Docker daemon. You can still write your own Dockerfile; buildpacks just give you a good default with no extra files.

steps.title: One jar, three environments
steps.problem: You have one `shop.jar`. Locally you want H2 and debug logging; staging and production both use PostgreSQL, with different URLs and passwords. How do you set this up without rebuilding?
steps: `application.properties`: shared defaults, e.g. `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info`.
`application-dev.properties`: the H2 URL and `logging.level.com.example=DEBUG`. Run locally with `./mvnw spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=dev`.
`application-prod.properties`: production settings such as logging levels and pool sizes, but **no secrets**.
Staging and production both run with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` and get their own `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` and `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD` from the platform's secret store.
steps.answer: Profiles for differences in behavior, environment variables for per-environment values and secrets: one artifact everywhere.

steps.prompt: Which command starts the packaged app on port 9000 without changing any file?
steps.explanation: Boot turns `--key=value` arguments into properties with the highest precedence. Without the leading `--` it is just an ordinary program argument, `-port` means nothing to Boot, and the `package` goal builds the jar rather than running it.
